Appendix E: Execution Steps 
The following steps summarize how the project can be executed during evaluation 
or demonstration. They are written for the local project folder and assume that 
Python dependencies are installed. 
8. Open the project folder adsb_tracker_2. 
9. Activate the Python environment or use the configured Python interpreter. 
10. Confirm that SIMULATION_MODE is true for replay-based demonstration. 
11. Run the Flask application using python app.py. 
12. Open http://localhost:5005 in a browser. 
13. Observe aircraft markers and select an aircraft to inspect details. 
14. Use the trajectory export endpoint if a CSV history export is required. 
15. Review generated SQLite, CSV and Excel files under the logs folder.

===== PAGE 78 =====
APPENDIX G: ALGORITHM SELECTION AND COMPARISON
G.1 Algorithm Used in the Project
The implemented predictor uses sliding-window ordinary least-squares linear regression. For each
aircraft, the latest stored samples are ordered by time. Separate straight lines are fitted for latitude,
longitude and altitude: value(t) = a + bt. The fitted lines are evaluated at the last sample time plus the
number of seconds for which the aircraft has been absent from the current feed.
Implemented constraints
•
Input window: up to the latest 20 stored trajectory points; at least 4 valid points are required.
•
Prediction condition: the aircraft must have been observed in the current session but be absent from the
current live/replay snapshot.
•
Prediction horizon: 1-180 seconds with the current configuration; older records are not displayed as
predictions.
•
Fallback: constant speed, heading and vertical rate are used when regression cannot be fitted.
•
Safety against feedback: predicted rows are output-only and are not written back into the training tables.
G.2 Why This Method Was Selected
For a local academic tracker, this method provides a useful balance: it is understandable, deterministic,
fast enough to run during every API refresh, and able to smooth small variations across several
observations. It needs no offline training dataset or GPU. Its main limitation is that a straight-line trend
cannot model a sharp turn or a prolonged outage, which is why the prediction age is deliberately
capped and the interface visually distinguishes predicted data from live data.
Recent stored
trajectory points
Validate age
and sample count
Fit latitude, longitude
and altitude vs. time
Extrapolate to
current outage age
Return predicted row
for dotted display

Last observation carried
forward
Keeps the last known position unchanged.
Almost no computation and works with
one record.
A moving aircraft immediately appears
stationary.
Poor; useful only as an emergency display
fallback.
Constant velocity and
heading
Moves the last position using current speed,
heading and vertical rate.
Very fast and does not require a training
dataset.
Does not smooth noise and cannot adapt
well to turns.
Good fallback; it is used when regression
cannot be fitted.
Sliding-window linear
regression (USED)
Fits straight lines to recent latitude, longitude
and altitude values over time.
Simple, explainable, smooths several
observations and is inexpensive.
Assumes locally straight motion; accuracy
drops during turns or long gaps.
Best present choice for short gaps, local
execution and limited data.
Kalman filter
Recursively estimates position and velocity
while modelling measurement noise.
Strong noise handling and efficient
real-time updates.
Needs a motion model and careful
covariance tuning.
Strong next upgrade when receiver-noise
statistics are available.
Polynomial regression
Fits a curved time trend instead of a straight
line.
Can represent gentle curvature over a
short window.
Higher-order extrapolation can become
unstable and overfit noise.
Conditional; requires strict order and
horizon controls.
Random forest / gradient
boosting
Learns nonlinear corrections from
engineered flight-state features.
Can model interactions that simple
formulas miss.
Requires representative labelled data and
does not naturally model sequence
continuity.
Research option after a larger verified
trajectory dataset is collected.
LSTM / GRU neural network
Learns temporal patterns from complete
sequences of prior flights.
Can model complex route and
manoeuvre patterns.
Needs substantial training data, tuning and
more computing power; less explainable.
Future work for large-scale historical
datasets, not the current local baseline.
Table 15: Trajectory Prediction Algorithm Comparison

Simulation Mode Dashboard
Figure 17: Simulation Mode Dashboard
•
Simulation TRUE means records are replayed from the configured captured log rather than received from the live

•
The same decoder, storage, prediction and interface pipeline is exercised, which makes repeatable testing possible
without receiver hardware.
